plan.topic: Plague in the US: about 7 human cases a year (CDC), mostly bubonic, mostly in the rural West
plan.angle: US-local number plus practical steps. CDC reports an average of 7 human cases a year (range 0–17). Most are in northern New Mexico, northern Arizona, southern Colorado, California, southern Oregon and far western Nevada, and over 80% are bubonic. Prevention from CDC: flea control on pets, don't handle sick or dead rodents, and see a doctor promptly with a fever after possible exposure in plague areas. Calm framing: rare, treatable, and monitored. Close with the line 'if you're worried, talk to a health professional'. Cite the CDC Maps and Statistics page with its last-reviewed date.

package.description:
CDC: the US sees about 7 human plague cases a year on average, mostly bubonic, mostly in two rural Western regions. In plague areas, ask your vet about flea control for pets and avoid touching sick or dead animals. Fever, chills or a painful swollen lymph node after possible exposure? Get medical care right away. If you're worried, talk to a health professional.

This content is for educational purposes only and is not medical advice. Always talk to a qualified healthcare professional about your own situation.

social.facebook_caption:
Yes, plague still exists in the US — about 7 human cases a year on average, per the CDC. It's rare, and most cases are bubonic, concentrated in two rural Western regions: northern New Mexico/Arizona plus southern Colorado, and California, southern Oregon and far western Nevada.

The usual route is a bite from an infected rodent flea. Outdoor cats and dogs can bring those fleas home, so CDC recommends flea control for pets (check with your vet on what's safe for your animal) and avoiding touching sick or dead animals (wear gloves if you must). If you get a fever, chills or a painful swollen lymph node after a possible exposure, seek care right away and mention it — plague can be cured with antibiotics, but treatment has to start quickly.

Curious how the reported Irkutsk, Russia case fits into all this? We break down what's confirmed vs. reported on our channel. If you're worried, talk to a health professional.

Had you heard plague was still around in the US?

factcheck.summary:
I checked all 4 cited CDC pages on Oct 7, 2026. They exist, their last-reviewed dates match the source list, and they support every factual claim in the script:
- An average of 7 human plague cases are reported each year in the US.
- Most cases come from 2 regions, listed word for word in s3.
- Cases occur in the rural West.
- Over 80% of US cases have been bubonic.
- Plague spreads to people through bites from infected rodent fleas.
- Plague can be cured with antibiotics, but treatment must be given quickly.
- Fever, chills and painful swollen lymph nodes mean you should seek immediate medical attention.
- Use flea control on pets, since pets that roam freely can bring fleas home.
- Wear gloves when handling potentially infected animals.

The Irkutsk case is correctly called 'reported', with no alarmist framing. The urgent-care line and the 'talk to a health professional' line are both present, and nothing stigmatises any group or region. The hook delivers what the title promises. I found 4 minor wording and safety tweaks; none needs a hold.

issues.claim: CDC advises flea control for cats and dogs
issues.problem: Some dog flea products (for example, permethrin spot-ons) are toxic to cats. Without a caveat, a viewer could use a dog product on a cat.
issues.fix: Narration: "pets that roam outdoors can bring those fleas home. In plague areas, CDC advises flea control for pets (ask your vet which product is safe for your cat or dog), and gloves if you ever handle sick or dead animals." List item 1: "Vet-approved flea control for pets"

issues.claim: On-screen text: "CDC: rare, mostly rural West"
issues.problem: The cited maps page doesn't use the word 'rare'. It gives the average of 7 cases and says the cases are rural and Western. Attributing 'rare' to CDC goes slightly beyond the source.
issues.fix: On-screen text: "CDC: mostly rural West" (keep "It's rare" in the narration as our own description).

issues.claim: gloves if you ever handle sick or dead animals
issues.problem: This closely paraphrases CDC's advice ('handling or skinning potentially infected animals') and is acceptable. Adding 'avoid touching' would better match CDC's wider prevention guidance.
issues.fix: Optional narration: "…and avoid touching sick or dead animals, or wear gloves if you must."

issues.claim: Got a fever, chills or a painful swollen lymph node after possible exposure?
issues.problem: These are bubonic symptoms only. Because the channel is focused on pneumonic plague, viewers may also need the respiratory red flag. This is optional, as the Short is about US bubonic cases.
issues.fix: Optional on-screen qualifier: "Fever + swollen node or cough? Get care now". Add a pneumonic line only if it is sourced to the CDC symptoms page.

audio.soundNotes: Music is already in the target window (-13.5 dB under speech, -13.9 dB in pauses) so left at unity; just thinned and tamed dense SFX clusters (dropped redundant ticks/blips near 10.6s, 19s and 38.4s, and one duplicate whoosh in the 'Worried?' beat) and pulled down a handful of cues that were poking above -14 dB during speech (opening ding/swoosh, the Yersinia-reveal bubble/blip, the 30.6s and 38.4s clusters, and the closing pop) so the voice stays clearly on top; dropped the near-inaudible swell at 33s as dead weight. Added three bespoke accents — a soft microscope pulse on the 'Yersinia pestis' label, a gentle heartbeat thump under 'Get care fast', and a warm reassuring pad on 'Worried?' — to add felt emotion at the key beats without competing with the narration.
